bet.text: A Feeder that rolls notes around the Turret, so the Shooter can keep tracking the goal and never has to line up with the Intake.

demand.text: The Shooter had to score in the Speaker from different distances and very accurately, because missed shots are costly. The Turret was for shooting on the move and faster alignment; the team also chose it early for shuttling notes and quick cleanup. The climb had to take under 2 seconds and reach the Trap.

auto.text: Branching autos: if a midline note is gone the robot goes to the next in a chosen priority order, then returns to score. Interviewed at the championship, the team was mostly running sprints: score the preload, go straight to the midline, and take the three close notes afterward.

cycle.text: The under-bumper Intake pulls in and centers a note. The Feeder rolls it around the Turret and stores it while the Turret tracks the Speaker, then accelerates it into the Shooter. For the amp, the note is sent up into the Amplifier and rolled out.

endgame.text: The first step raises the climber arms. One button then raises the elevator, pulls the robot up, moves the note to its staged position and releases it into the Trap.

fallback.text: A Human Player can feed notes into the raised Amplifier, an alternate intake path for the passing strategy.
After losing the first Einstein final, an alliance partner's driver says, 254 and 1323 both cycled from the source, which worked better against defense.

gave_up.text: The Turret's energy chain was a big constraint on where electronics could go, and the climber's jackshaft had to run through a hole in the Turret's tubing. Heavy shooter wheels chosen for inertia made the robot very overweight.
Better trap scoring cost the earlier amp mechanism its backward trick shot, which never ran at competition.

changed.text: Between Sacramento and East Bay nearly the whole shooter was redesigned because of spin-up time: another motor, more rollers and a straighter path. Machined inertia flywheels then replaced heavy wheels.

A team member, in their own opinion, would change the strategy calls, not the alliance pick: in the Einstein finals the team pivoted one match late, then lost its one chance at the new strategy to a tech foul.

outcome.text: 45-5-1 in official play; won the Newton division; championship finalist; captain of the Newton alliance on Einstein; ranked 15 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 53.89, Newton).

solves.text: Maneuver quickly, avoid defense and resist tipping

facts.text: The binder gives SDS MK4i modules at an L3 reduction and 18 ft/s; the interview says the drive pinion was swapped to 13 teeth, which draws less current with little effect on speed
Square frame side
3x1 tubes put the bellypan 1/2 in above the floor and keep notes out of the modules
Krakens on every subsystem; motor count
A 1x1 solid 7075 bar and a 1/4 in plate stiffen the bumper in front of the Intake
Weight at the championship, with the new radio
1/4 in plates with threaded holes sit inside the drive tubes, so subsystems bolt on without nuts, and double as crush spacers for the swerve module screws
Rear bumpers mount with aluminum blocks and a 1/4-20 screw through the rear swerve modules; in front, where space was short, two 5/16-18 adhesive-mount studs slot into an intake crossbar

solves.text: Pick up several notes without jamming and survive collisions in the autonomous race to the midline

cost.text: Among the most iterated subsystems, because it is so tightly integrated with the shooter, carriage and Amplifier

facts.text: Mecanum and sideways funneling wheels let notes come in from the sides
Surface speed, about, from one Kraken
A one-way spring ramp lets notes in from below, then sends them up to the Amplifier on exhaust
In general a note sticks between the top and bottom rollers as the robot drives into it, even with the Intake off

solves.text: Take notes from the Intake to the Shooter with the Turret at any position

facts.text: A flat box the team calls the "pizza box": rollers drag a note around it, squished horizontally, and up a ramp into the Shooter
Two Krakens allow a direction switch, which prevents jams and takes the shortest path to the Shooter
It stores a note and accelerates it into the Shooter when ready
Mounted on top of the swerve modules with velcro, so it comes off for servicing
Based on the team's 2020 robot, and prototyped early

solves.text: Track the Speaker continuously, separate from the rest of the robot

cost.text: The energy chain was a big constraint on electronics placement

facts.text: Range of motion
A 3D printed energy chain, with a custom profile for its wires, is tensioned by a constant force spring
Two encoders geared 1:1 and 1:2.3 give position through multiple wraps
One Kraken through 14:52 and 10:125 reductions
The energy chain was laid out first on a table with the bellypan, electronics and turret wrap marked, to find its link count and tensioner position
Its links copy an existing chain model, resized with stronger tabs, and were printed on an HP Multi Jet Fusion machine in a batch of about one day, enough for two robots and spares

functions.name: Shooter

cost.text: Heavy wheels gave the inertia but made the robot very overweight, until flywheels replaced them

functions.type: quad-flywheel shooter with an adjustable hood

facts.text: The Hood covers launch angles from 10 to 50 degrees above horizontal
One Kraken drives the feed rollers; after them one drives the top flywheel rollers and one the bottom
Unequal wheels put spin on the note so it travels flatter and farther
Shims between gears and hex shafts remove Hood backlash
Inertia flywheels on the shaft ends help when shooting many notes in a row
The published code counts a shot as on target only when flywheel speed is within 4 percent of its set point, Turret and Hood are within tolerance and the set point is valid
The back of the note path is a fixed 1/32 in bent aluminum sheet; a nylon printed ramp behind it moves with the Hood and supports it; both are covered in Teflon tape
Low-infill printed cylinders with cat-tongue grip tape replaced the prototype's solid rubber wheels, and large-diameter aluminum flywheels put the lost inertia back for less weight
Stage 1 uses treaded wheels, a material that does not clog with dust from the note's skin
The team says it needed the inertia because the Turret shoots several notes in a row, with two flywheel motors where some teams used four

solves.text: Redirect notes down into the Amp or Trap, and take notes from the Human Player

cost.text: Removing cat-tongue tape from the bottom roller made the trap more consistent but lost a backward trick shot that never ran at competition
Falls while climbing bent the elevator uprights, which were easy to replace
The team normally keeps subsystems self-contained, easier to upgrade or fix; packaging the elevator and Intake together was not the intent

facts.text: Elevator range
The elevator covers that range in under
A note is sent between two rollers like chopsticks, then scored at an angle by reversing them
Passive wheels roll against the stage while the robot climbs
For the trap, roller power is pulsed
The elevator can also block opponents
Moving carriage with rollers, gearbox and motor
Two 110T 5 mm HTD belts lift the carriage, joined by a jackshaft because driving one side of so wide an elevator could rack it
That jackshaft runs inside the 3 in intake roller, which spins freely on it: a live and a dead axle at once
Carriage plates are 1/4 in aluminum, pocketed part way to leave a smooth 0.030 in web for the Teflon guides
Bearings on screws guide the carriage front to back; 1/8 in Teflon bar guides it side to side
Solid-infill printed blocks with teeth join belt to carriage and lasted the season at low load; the team would use metal, rope or chain for climbing loads
Pressed-in pins, about 1/16 in, keep the printed layers from shearing apart
For service the belt is slackened and slid out, and the whole carriage lifts out of the tubes

functions.name: Climber

solves.text: Lift the robot high enough for the Amplifier to reach the Trap

functions.type: winched hook arms on gas springs

facts.text: Lift height
Winch time, about
15 lb gas springs lift the arms; Dyneema on a hex jackshaft winches both sides down
One Kraken's brake mode holds the arms down after the match

solves.text: Split operator controls by the part of the game being played

facts.text: Speaker mode tracks the goal by Limelight; other modes handle the amp, human player loading and passing
The passing set point changes once the robot crosses the opposing alliance's wing line
The note is always staged in the shooter, and moved up for the amp only when needed

functions.name: Branching autos

solves.text: Keep scoring when a wanted midline note is already gone

functions.type: split trajectories that branch on the fly

facts.text: Selectors set the start location and the order of midline notes
Optimized trajectories are split so the path can change during the run

functions.name: Localization

solves.text: Know where the robot is for aiming, with the best estimate available at each moment

functions.type: Limelight AprilTag methods switched by heuristics

facts.text: Three methods: Megatag, the only one allowed to correct gyro yaw; Megatag2, the main one by the end of the year; and a pinhole model
Pinhole position error from the wing line and beyond, one camera, with a very accurate camera height and pitch, generally under
Megatag1 with one Limelight routinely had errors above this at similar range, with much more jitter
The pinhole model is less sensitive to pixel noise but relies on a good estimate of camera pitch, roll, yaw and height
Measurements taken while the camera turns at a non-negligible rate are thrown out
After almost every match the team searched logs for bad position updates and found ways to reject them

cost.text: Camera calibration often drifted after a few matches, though the lens glue showed no failure, and recalibrating improved results
A camera on the Turret adds time synchronization problems as it whips around; a team member says they might argue for more frame-mounted cameras if doing it again
Megatag2 lagged because the gyro yaw it was given was not time-synced precisely; the effect was small, because the Turret kept the camera facing the goal

decisions.because: the Shooter can track the goal without interruption, which makes aiming faster and shooting on the move reliable
decisions.instead_of: a turret that must align with the Intake as a note comes in

decisions.choice: Put the Shooter on a Turret
decisions.because: it allows shooting on the move and faster alignment, and helps shuttling and cleanup
it is robust to collisions, especially in the autonomous race to the midline
they lower the center of gravity and keep the robot from running notes into the swerve modules
they keep the moment of inertia while staying light

decisions.choice: Pulse the rollers when scoring the trap
decisions.because: it pushes the note in slowly and is more consistent
the team expected many counter autos

decisions.choice: Intake surface speed below drive speed
decisions.because: it puts the motor at a good part of its torque curve while it compresses and bends the note, and the usual rule does not hold for objects that do not roll
plates are much lighter with fewer parts, hold rollers and bearings directly, and are easily changed for new roller positions
gearing them up would add bearings, shaft weight and complexity, and that much inertia was not needed
decisions.instead_of: flywheels geared faster than the wheels

decisions.because: they can be lighter, put the motor lower through belts, fit unusual spaces, and avoid the tiny gears and possible binding of planetaries
they mostly work once mounted, which frees limited software people
decisions.cost: work to learn, integrate and get support for a bought part

decisions.choice: Vendor swerve class and WPILib commands
decisions.because: the vendor class gave 95 percent of what the team wanted, already tested; commands come with training material most teams share
decisions.instead_of: the team's own swerve kinematics and subsystem manager

decisions.choice: Build a strong base, then borrow mechanisms
decisions.because: the team calls prototyping a weakness and complex integration and adapting through the season strengths
decisions.instead_of: committing to a design from early prototypes

decisions.because: it had shown better auto, endgame, interchangeable roles, solo cycling and consistency
decisions.instead_of: 2910, probably the best passer at its best
